results.result: Action potential-independent miniature spontaneous Ca2+ transients (mSCTs) occur in hippocampal neurons under physiological Mg2+ concentrations and can be detected using multiple Ca2+ indicator probes with varying efficiencies. Fluo-4 AM detects mSCTs at 0.32 ± 0.04 min⁻¹ per ROI, with kinetics showing mean rise time of 0.38 s and decay time of 0.86 s. The detection efficiency varies by probe type, with postsynaptically-targeted GCaMP5K-PSD95 showing the lowest detection rate (0.009 ± 0.004 min⁻¹) in physiological Mg2+, suggesting mSCTs are not primarily localized to the postsynaptic density and involve amplification mechanisms downstream of initial Ca2+ influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C24-C40 provide comprehensive characterization of mSCTs using multiple complementary imaging approaches (Fluo-4 AM, whole-cell Fluo-4, soluble GCaMP5K, GCaMP5K-PSD95). The data include quantitative measurements of frequency, kinetics, and amplitude with appropriate statistical analyses. The observation that mSCT amplitude is unaffected by Mg2+ despite its effect on NMDA receptor currents (C28, C29) provides strong evidence for an amplification mechanism. The differential detection by various probes (C30-C36) supports the conclusion about subcellular localization.

results.result: mSCTs require Ca2+ influx through NMDA receptors. Removal of extracellular Ca2+ or blockade of NMDA receptors with AP5 significantly reduces mSCT frequency (p = 0.038 for both conditions), demonstrating that NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ entry is critical for mSCT generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C41-C44 demonstrate through pharmacological manipulation that both extracellular Ca2+ and NMDA receptor activity are required for mSCTs. The experiments use appropriate controls (sequential application of 0 mM Ca2+, 2 mM Ca2+, and 2 mM Ca2+ + AP5) with statistical validation (one-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak's multiple comparisons). The virtual absence of mSCTs in nominal Ca2+ conditions provides strong evidence for the requirement of Ca2+ influx.

results.result: mSCT frequency correlates with spontaneous neurotransmitter release. Hypertonic sucrose increases both mEPSC frequency (2.6-fold) and mSCT frequency (2.3-fold). SNAP-25 knockout neurons, which have diminished spontaneous release, show significantly decreased mSCT frequency that remains sensitive to AP5, demonstrating that mSCTs are driven by spontaneous vesicular glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C45-C55 provide converging evidence from two complementary approaches: acute manipulation with hypertonic sucrose and genetic manipulation with SNAP-25 knockout. The parallel changes in mEPSC and mSCT frequencies with sucrose (C46, C47) provide strong correlative evidence. The SNAP-25 KO experiments (C53-C55) provide genetic validation, with the continued AP5 sensitivity in KO neurons supporting the NMDA receptor dependence. The cited literature on SNAP-25 KO phenotype (C49-C52) is appropriately referenced.

results.result: AMPA receptors do not contribute to mSCTs. Treatment with the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (5 µM) does not affect mSCT frequency, ruling out both direct contributions from Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors and indirect contributions via local depolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C59-C60 demonstrate through pharmacological blockade that AMPA receptors are not required for mSCTs. The experiment uses appropriate before/after design with statistical analysis (p = 0.78, paired t-test). The interpretation (C60) appropriately considers both direct (Ca2+-permeable receptors) and indirect (depolarization-mediated) mechanisms. Background claims C56-C58 provide appropriate context from the literature.

results.result: L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels do not contribute to mSCT generation. Nimodipine (5 µM) does not affect mSCT frequency (p = 0.89), though L-type channels may still influence resting Ca2+ levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C61-C62 demonstrate through pharmacological blockade with nimodipine that L-type Ca2+ channels do not contribute to mSCT generation. The statistical analysis is appropriate (paired t-test, N=7). The caveat in C63 about potential effects on resting Ca2+ levels is appropriately noted and supported by citation. Figure 4—figure supplement 1 validates that nimodipine is effective in this system by showing ~27% reduction in action potential-evoked Ca2+ influx.

results.result: Group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1 and mGluR5) do not contribute to mSCTs. Combined application of mGluR1 antagonist YM202074 and mGluR5 antagonist Fenobam does not significantly change mSCT frequency (p = 0.26).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C64-C65 demonstrate through dual pharmacological blockade that group I mGluRs are not required for mSCTs. The statistical analysis is appropriate (paired t-test, N=8). Figure 4—figure supplement 2 validates drug efficacy by showing blockade of DHPG-induced Ca2+ responses. Background claim C66 provides appropriate mechanistic context from the literature.

results.result: mSCTs require Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) from ryanodine receptor (RyR)-gated internal stores. Dantrolene significantly reduces mSCT frequency (p = 0.008), and ryanodine produces a ~5-fold decrease in mSCT frequency (p = 0.004) with substantial reduction in amplitude. Under physiological Mg2+ concentrations with ryanodine blockade, Fluo-4 cannot detect NMDA-mediated Ca2+ transients, demonstrating that CICR amplification is essential for mSCT detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C22, C67-C75 provide strong evidence for CICR involvement using two complementary RyR blockers (dantrolene and ryanodine) with appropriate statistical analyses. The use-dependent protocol for ryanodine (C72) is methodologically sound. The amplitude reduction after ryanodine (C73) and the inability to detect transients in physiological Mg2+ after RyR blockade (C75) provide compelling evidence for the amplification mechanism. Background claims C67-C69, C71 appropriately cite prior literature on CICR mechanisms and drug actions.

results.result: Inhibition of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release with ryanodine elicits homeostatic synaptic scaling. Treatment with TTX + ryanodine for 3 hours produces a significant rightward shift in mEPSC amplitude distributions with a scaling factor of 1.28 (28% increase), similar to the positive control TTX + AP5. This scaling effect is postsynaptic, as acute ryanodine application does not alter mEPSC frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C23, C82-C88 demonstrate synaptic scaling through multiple lines of evidence: cumulative probability distributions showing rightward shifts (C82-C83), rank-order analysis revealing multiplicative scaling (C84), and appropriate positive control with AP5 (C83). The observation that acute ryanodine doesn't affect mEPSC frequency (C87) supports the postsynaptic interpretation (C88). Background claims C76-C81 provide appropriate context on synaptic scaling mechanisms from the literature. The scaling factor is smaller than with AP5 (C85), which is appropriately explained by incomplete mSCT blockade (C86).

results.result: Synaptic scaling induced by ryanodine requires protein synthesis. Pretreatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin (20 µM) completely abolishes the increase in mEPSC amplitudes induced by TTX + ryanodine treatment, with no significant difference in amplitude distributions compared to TTX alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C91 demonstrate protein synthesis dependence through pharmacological blockade with anisomycin. The experimental design with 30-minute pretreatment is appropriate. Statistical analysis shows no significant difference between vehicle and ryanodine groups when anisomycin is present (Figure 5E, p = 0.078 by Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). Background claims C89-C90 appropriately cite prior work establishing protein synthesis requirements for synaptic scaling.

results.result: Synaptic scaling induced by ryanodine requires eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF2) kinase activity. In wild-type neurons, TTX + ryanodine produces a 42% increase in synaptic strength, but in eEF2 kinase knockout neurons, the same treatment produces only a 1% difference, demonstrating that RyR-dependent mSCT signaling acts through Ca2+-dependent eEF2 kinase to maintain synaptic homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C93-C97 provide strong genetic evidence for eEF2 kinase requirement using knockout mice. The wild-type controls show robust scaling (42% increase, C94) while knockouts show no scaling (1% difference, C96), with appropriate statistical analyses (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests). The use of littermate controls (C93) is methodologically sound. Background claim C92 appropriately cites prior work on eEF2 kinase regulation. The conclusion (C97) is well-supported by the genetic loss-of-function data.

results.result: Spontaneous glutamate release-driven NMDA receptor activity maintains synaptic homeostasis through Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release amplification. The detected mSCT rate (0.32 ± 0.03 min⁻¹) is lower than the spontaneous release rate (0.76 ± 0.03 min⁻¹), suggesting not all release events generate mSCTs. The amplification via internal stores produces delocalized, pulsatile Ca2+ signals that may allow synaptic NMDA receptors to influence dendritic regions where eEF2 localizes, providing a mechanistic link between spontaneous neurotransmission and synaptic efficacy control.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12, C98-C111 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The comparison of mSCT and release rates (C98-C100) is appropriately cautious in interpretation. The localization arguments (C101, C108) are supported by both the imaging data with different probes and cited literature on ER and eEF2 localization. The functional significance claims (C105-C107, C111) are reasonable inferences from the data, though some aspects remain speculative (C107, C110). The comparison with evoked release (C104) appropriately cites prior work (C102-C103) and notes differences.

results.result: Prior work has established that spontaneous neurotransmitter release triggers biochemical signaling for synaptic maturation, stability, and homeostatic plasticity, with NMDA receptors signaling at rest under physiological Mg2+ concentrations. Under these conditions, mEPSCs possess a sizable NMDA receptor component representing ~20% of unblocked NMDA receptor Ca2+ influx, and blockade of spontaneous release or NMDA receptors induces faster synaptic scaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C21 appropriately summarize prior literature that provides context for the current study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed work (Chung and Kavalali 2006; Sutton et al. 2006, 2007; Kavalali 2015; Nosyreva et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2011; Espinosa and Kavalali 2009; Povysheva and Johnson 2012; Gideons et al. 2014; Jahr and Stevens 1990). These background claims establish the rationale for investigating the properties of resting Ca2+ signals.
